records.place: Simonsberg-Stellenbosch ward, Stellenbosch district, Western Cape

wine.name: Kanonkop Paul Sauer
wine.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, from about three fifths to three quarters by year, with Cabernet Franc and Merlot making up the rest, their parts moving too.
wine.sites: Kanonkop's own vineyards on the lower slopes of the Simonsberg, in decomposed granite.
wine.making: Fermented in open concrete fermenters, the cap of skins punched down by hand every two hours through the ferment, as the house describes it. The wine then matures for about two years in new French oak barriques, Nevers oak in the house's recent notes, before it is bottled.
wine.glass: Cassis, plum and sour cherry over cedar, cigar box and tobacco leaf; full and firm, with a dense, fine tannin that takes years to soften and a long, dry finish.
wine.ageing: Firm and closed in its youth, it is made to be kept: a strong vintage needs a decade or more in bottle before it opens.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour or two, an old one gently off its sediment; a Bordeaux glass.

label.means: Honours the cabinet minister who owned the farm and died in 1976.
The ward on the Simonsberg's lower slopes within the Stellenbosch district; every grape must have grown in it.

records.table: Named for the cabinet minister who owned the farm, Kanonkop's Paul Sauer is a Cabernet led Bordeaux blend from the Simonsberg, first made in 1981. Open concrete tanks for the ferment and two years in new French oak leave it firm and cedary, so decant it.
records.story: The house traces its name to a hillock on the Simonsberg above the farm, where in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries a cannon was fired to announce sailing ships entering Table Bay. After the First World War the farm passed to Paul Sauer (1898 to 1976), son of a Cape cabinet minister and himself a minister in the National Party governments from 1948 into the 1960s. In 1973 his son-in-law and the estate's winemaker bottled the first wines under the Kanonkop label, Cabernet Sauvignon and Pinotage among them; Sauer, who had long sold the farm's grapes in bulk to the Stellenbosch Farmers' Winery, was uneasy at first, by the house's account. He died in 1976, and the farm passed to his daughter, who had married into the Krige family. With the 1981 vintage the estate made its first Bordeaux blend and gave it his name: Paul Sauer, Cabernet Sauvignon with Cabernet Franc and Merlot, fermented in open concrete tanks with the cap punched down by hand and aged in new French oak. Though the house is known above all for Pinotage, Paul Sauer holds none of the grape. On a list it is the Stellenbosch Cabernet blend to name first, and the proof that Kanonkop is more than its Pinotage.

wine.name: Meerlust Rubicon
wine.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon leads, from under half to about seven tenths of the blend by year, with Merlot, Cabernet Franc and, in later vintages, a little Petit Verdot.
wine.sites: The estate's own vineyards in the cool south of Stellenbosch near False Bay: weathered granite on the warm Compagniesdrift hill, clay of an old estuary on the lowlands, shale at the Quarry, sand and river stones on the terraces.
wine.making: Each parcel of each variety is fermented apart, with pump overs and délestage, and goes through malolactic fermentation in 300 litre French oak barrels, mostly Nevers and more than half new in the vintages whose sheets give a share. After about eight months the components are blended and returned to barrel, for sixteen to twenty one months in all; the wine then rests in bottle before release.
wine.glass: Violet, ripe plum, blackberry and cassis over cedar, fennel and liquorice; restrained rather than heavy, with fine, firm tannin and a dry finish that, with age, turns towards tobacco leaf and cigar box.
wine.ageing: Opens after some years in bottle and develops for a decade and more, longer in a strong vintage.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius, in a Bordeaux glass; an hour in a decanter suits a young bottle, while an old one is decanted gently off its sediment.

label.means: Named for crossing the Rubicon, a step with no turning back.
A district under Wine of Origin, and all the bottle's grapes grew inside it.
Certification, since 1973, of the origin, vintage and variety the label claims, with a seal on the neck.

records.table: The Myburgh family bought Meerlust, near False Bay, in 1756, and its Rubicon, from the 1980 vintage, is a blend led by Cabernet Sauvignon with Merlot and Cabernet Franc. Violet, plum and cedar come with restraint rather than weight, and it rewards years in bottle.
records.story: In 1693, the estate records, a German settler took up the farm and named it Meerlust, the pleasure of the sea, since by the estate's account the homestead stands on a granite outcrop five kilometres from False Bay. In 1756 the Myburgh family bought it, eight generations by their own count. The front of the homestead was completed in 1776, and the farmstead has since been declared a national monument. For more than two centuries Meerlust sold its grapes and wine in bulk; the seventh generation of the family turned it towards bottling under the estate's own name, beginning with a Cabernet Sauvignon in the 1970s. Drawn to Bordeaux, he and his winemaker set out to blend Cabernet Sauvignon with Merlot and Cabernet Franc in the Médoc manner, and the 1980 vintage became Rubicon, among the first Bordeaux blends of the modern Cape. The poet D. J. Opperman (1914 to 1985), a friend and a professor at the University of Stellenbosch, suggested the name, in the estate's telling: like crossing the Rubicon, the decision could not be undone. At his death in 1988 his son, the eighth generation, took over. Rubicon came in the first generation of Cape Bordeaux blends, and it is a wine made to be kept.

wine.name: Rustenberg John X Merriman
wine.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot lead, their balance shifting from year to year, with smaller parts of Petit Verdot and Malbec and, in some earlier years, Cabernet Franc.
wine.sites: Decomposed granite on the Simonsberg slopes above Stellenbosch, in the estate's own vineyards and no others.
wine.making: Stainless steel tanks take the ferment, with about a week of extended maceration on the skins. Ageing follows in French oak barriques, around a third of them new and the rest second and third fill, for about twenty months before bottling.
wine.glass: Sour cherry and blackcurrant with cigar tobacco over fine grained tannin; with age the tannin softens and the palate turns rounder and more savoury.
wine.ageing: Worth decanting in its youth; the house gives it ten to fifteen years from the vintage in a good cellar.
wine.serve: Serve at 16 to 18 degrees Celsius, decanting a young bottle an hour ahead and an old one off its sediment with care; a Bordeaux glass.

records.table: Granted in 1682, the Simonsberg farm of Rustenberg makes John X Merriman, a Bordeaux blend that carries the name of the Cape prime minister who farmed Schoongezicht from 1892. Cabernet and Merlot from decomposed granite give cassis, sour cherry and cigar tobacco.
records.story: A grant of 1682 to a German settler from near the Rhine began the farm, by the estate's history. In 1810 an owner divided it into two farms, Rustenberg and Schoongezicht. Phylloxera struck the Cape's vineyards in the late nineteenth century, and in 1892 John X Merriman (1841 to 1926), the English born politician who would be the last prime minister of the Cape Colony, from 1908 to 1910, took on Schoongezicht, while his brother-in-law took Rustenberg; together they replanted on resistant rootstock. Wine has been bottled at the estate without a break since 1892, on its own record. In 1941 the Barlow family bought Rustenberg, and later added Schoongezicht, joining the two farms again after more than a century apart. The estate's Bordeaux blend carries Merriman's name and draws only on its own vineyards; beside it the single vineyard Peter Barlow Cabernet honours the buyer of 1941. A bottle of John X Merriman ties a Simonsberg red to a Cape prime minister, and to an estate that has bottled its own wine for well over a century.

wine.name: Simonsig Kaapse Vonkel Brut
wine.appellation: Stellenbosch or Western Cape, by vintage
wine.grapes: Chardonnay and Pinot Noir in roughly equal parts, with a little Pinot Meunier and, in some years, a touch of Pinot Blanc; the first vintage, of 1971, was Chenin Blanc.
wine.sites: Chardonnay and Pinot Noir from Stellenbosch, and in the vintages labelled Western Cape from vineyards beyond the district as well.
wine.making: The juice is fermented in stainless steel at a cool 15 to 17 degrees Celsius, part of the Chardonnay in older French oak barrels, and malolactic fermentation is avoided to keep it fresh. The second fermentation takes place in the bottle, and the wine rests at least twenty months on its lees before disgorging.
wine.glass: Green apple and ripe pear with shortbread from the lees, a fine, lively mousse, fresh, crisp acidity and a delicate, dry finish with a stony edge.
wine.ageing: Made to be drunk on release, while its fruit is fresh; kept a few years more it softens and gains toasty depth.
wine.serve: 8 to 10 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a tulip shaped white wine glass shows it better than a narrow flute.

records.table: Simonsig's Kaapse Vonkel, Cape sparkle, is the wine from which South Africa dates Cap Classique, sparkling wine fermented again in the bottle. First made from Chenin Blanc of the 1971 harvest, it has been led by Chardonnay and Pinot Noir since 1987, with twenty months and more on its lees.
records.story: In 1953, the family recalls, Simonsig's founder began to farm on De Hoop, which he rented from his father-in-law, and in the early 1960s he bought land of his own. In 1968 he bottled the first wine under the Simonsig name, a Chenin Blanc labelled Steen. Taken with the method of Champagne, he made from the 1971 harvest a sparkling wine fermented a second time in its bottle. The Cape grew little Chardonnay or Pinot Noir then, so the wine was Chenin Blanc. He called it Kaapse Vonkel, Cape sparkle, and released it in 1973. Earlier Cape cellars had tried the method, but the Cap Classique producers count Kaapse Vonkel as the first wine of their category. In 1971, too, Simonsig was among the estates that founded the Stellenbosch Wine Route. In 1987 the blend moved to Pinot Noir and Chardonnay, and Pinot Meunier later joined them. As other cellars took up the method, the style took the name Méthode Cap Classique, and in 1992 its makers formed an association. When a guest asks about Cap Classique, the Cape's own name for the traditional method, Kaapse Vonkel is the bottle to begin with, since the category counts its years from it.

wine.name: Lanzerac Pinotage
wine.grapes: Pinotage, unblended: the Cape's own crossing of Pinot Noir and Cinsaut, made at Stellenbosch in 1925.
wine.sites: Mainly the estate's own blocks in the Jonkershoek Valley on the edge of Stellenbosch town, where mountain soils and a mountain climate keep structure and natural acidity in the grapes, by the house's notes.
wine.making: After fermentation on the skins, malolactic fermentation follows in barrel, and the wine matures for at least fifteen months in a careful mix of new, second fill and third fill French oak barrels, racked regularly along the way.
wine.glass: Ripe plum and red and black berries with a hint of sweet oak; a rounded, generous mouthfeel, soft tannin and a lingering finish, with chocolate and caramel as it ages.
wine.ageing: Approachable from release, by the house's notes; it keeps for three to ten years by vintage, gaining notes of chocolate and caramel.
wine.serve: 15 to 17 degrees Celsius; a young bottle needs no decanting, though an hour of air does no harm; a Bordeaux glass.

label.means: The Cape's own grape, Pinot Noir crossed with Cinsaut, then called Hermitage, in 1925.
The estate's name since 1920, when a new owner renamed the farm once called Schoongezicht.
The district named on the label, home of the estate and of the university where Pinotage was bred.

records.table: The first label to say Pinotage, on the 1959 vintage sold in 1961, carried the name of Lanzerac, an estate of the Jonkershoek Valley. Its Lanzerac Pinotage, mainly from its own valley vineyards and matured in French oak, gives ripe plum and berries with a soft, rounded finish.
records.story: Lanzerac's land was granted in 1692 to a settler who named the farm Schoongezicht and, the estate relates, planted its first vines. In 1920 a new owner bought the farm and renamed it Lanzerac; the story goes that the name honours a French general of the First World War, a tale told rather than recorded. In 1925, at the university in Stellenbosch, Abraham Perold (1880 to 1941), its first professor of viticulture, crossed Pinot Noir with Cinsaut, then called Hermitage, and gave the Cape its own grape. The first wine sold as Pinotage came from the 1959 vintage, from grapes grown and made at the Bellevue farm, by most accounts. It was judged the champion of the young wine show that year, and the Stellenbosch Farmers' Winery released it in 1961 under its Lanzerac label, in the Pinotage Association's account. The estate counts that label as its own heritage, and its Lanzerac Pinotage, from its own Jonkershoek vineyards, carries the name forward. The lesson lies in the detail: the first Pinotage label said Lanzerac, but by most accounts the grapes grew at Bellevue.

others.name: Lanzerac Pionier Pinotage
others.note: The estate's other Pinotage, basket pressed and aged up to twenty two months in barriques, up to half of them new.

traps: By most accounts Bellevue grew the grapes of the first wine labelled Pinotage; the Lanzerac name on it was a label of the Stellenbosch Farmers' Winery.
Pinotage was crossed in 1925 from Pinot Noir and Cinsaut; Hermitage was the old Cape name for Cinsaut, not Syrah.
The 1959 is the vintage of the first Pinotage label; 1961 is the year it reached the market.

cards.front: Lanzerac Pinotage: which two grapes were crossed to make Pinotage, by whom and in which year?
cards.back: Pinot Noir and Cinsaut, then called Hermitage at the Cape, crossed by Abraham Perold in 1925.

cards.front: On the first label to say Pinotage, the 1959 vintage sold in 1961, whose grapes and whose name were they?
cards.back: By most accounts grapes from the Bellevue farm; the name Lanzerac, a label of the Stellenbosch Farmers' Winery.

questions.exp: The house's notes say the grapes come mainly from Lanzerac's own Jonkershoek Valley blocks; Bellevue, by most accounts, grew the grapes of the first Pinotage of 1959, not of this wine.

questions.q: The 1959 that first named Pinotage on its label reached the market in what year?
questions.exp: The Stellenbosch Farmers' Winery released it in 1961 under the Lanzerac label; 1925 is the year of the crossing and 1941 the year the first barrel of Pinotage wine was made.

report: Swap proposed, to Vergelegen (its V or GVB Red) or Warwick (Trilogy): the Pinotage Association and Bellevue's own page tell it that the first Pinotage of 1959 was grown and made at Bellevue and released in 1961 by the Stellenbosch Farmers' Winery under its Lanzerac label, so the estate's claim is to a merchant's label rather than its own vineyard, and the plan's why overstates it.
Lanzerac is better known as a hotel than as a wine house, Kanonkop already carries Pinotage for the group, and the region record itself names Vergelegen among the houses to name.

The Codex's region summary and producers line say Lanzerac sold the 1959 Pinotage in 1961; the record follows the Pinotage Association, that it was the merchant's Lanzerac label with Bellevue's grapes, hedged as most accounts because one account says the 1959 also held fruit from Kanonkop.
Founded is empty: the estate dates itself to 1692, and a Stellenbosch heritage survey (stellenboschheritage.co.za, Lanzerac historical property) dates the first grant to 1683.

The year of the purchase and renaming is 1920 in the estate's pages and the heritage survey, 1922 in one other account; the survey links the name to a French village, the estate to a rumour of General Lanrezac, so the story keeps the estate's rumour; the survey's reason for the renaming and the hotel of the late 1950s rest on one source each and are left out.
The first grantee and the owner of 1920 are described, not named, since their dates were not found in two sources.
The fermentation vessel differs by vintage in the house's notes (open wooden fermenters, stainless steel), so making says so; the 1996 planting of the Pionier block is the house's own account.

changed: founded: was empty; now 1692, the estate's own year and the grant of 28 February 1692 in the Stellenbosch heritage time line of the Jonkershoek Valley, with Daily Maverick's 330 years of 2022 agreeing; the 1683 of the survey's property sheet is set against it in the review.
wine.sites and questions[0]: the grapes come mainly from the estate's own Jonkershoek blocks, as the house's 2023 page says, not wholly.

wine.making: the open wooden fermenters or steel and the pump overs are cut, in no note read; malolactic in barrel and at least fifteen months in new, second and third fill French oak with regular racking stand on the house's 2023 page.
wine.ageing: three to ten years by vintage, since the house's listings give three to six years for the 2023 and five to ten in another.
table: mainly from its own valley vineyards, as the sites now say.
story: the founding is told as a grant of 1692 on two sources; the first vines stay the estate's account.

others[0]: the Pionier block planted in 1996 and the single vineyard are cut, in no source read; basket pressed and up to twenty two months in barriques, up to half new, from the house's Pionier page.
questions[1].exp: the first barrel of 1941 is no longer said to be made at Elsenburg; the accounts read say a lecturer of the university made it, and only one ties the vines to Elsenburg.
sources: the house's Pinotage 2023 page and the heritage time line replace the 2022 note and Bellevue's page, which stay in the review with Decanter's Wine Legend.
open: The year of the crossing: 1925 by the Codex, the Pinotage Association and most accounts; some give the pollination as 17 November 1924 and the seeds sown in 1925.
The 1959 wine: Bellevue's grapes alone by most accounts, with Kanonkop fruit by one, and a little Cinsaut by others.
The renaming: the estate's rumour of General Lanrezac stands as a tale; the heritage time line gives a French village the owner liked and a wish to avoid confusion with another farm.
The swap to Vergelegen or Warwick was refused; the plan's why should say the 1961 label was the Stellenbosch Farmers' Winery's Lanzerac brand.
